openItems.explanation: The June 26 off-cycle bonus run (PR-2614), $20,207.60, was deposited July 7, 8 calendar days after its June 29 due date: $1,010.38 at 5% is owed on the actual paydays even after the Schedule B. The reply asks for the Automatic Exemption from Penalty on the clean twelve-quarter history. The reasonable-cause statement drafted as a fallback is weak: off-cycle runs are not in the payroll system's automatic deposit batch and this one's deposit was not scheduled, an oversight, and the IRS says mistakes and reliance on others generally do not qualify. A person decides whether to send it; if sent, the President signs it under penalty of perjury.

For 2026 quarterly returns the IRS applies the Automatic Exemption from Penalty, not First Time Abate. On the client's records Q2 2023 to Q1 2026 qualify: all twelve returns on time and paid, all deposits by EFTPS, and the one penalty (Q1 2024, $2,372.18) abated for reasonable cause, which does not count. AEP is applied when the original return processes, and no AEP letter came for Q2; whether the IRS will apply it to the remaining penalty after the Schedule B, and how many FTD waivers its own records show (four or more disqualify), are for a person to confirm with the IRS once Form 2848 is on file.

The payroll system's Form 941 setting has said monthly since its May 4, 2026 upgrade, and it still does. The Q3 2026 return is being prepared separately with a Schedule B; a person confirms it went in that way (otherwise a CP207 for Q3 will follow), switches the setting back to semiweekly before the Q4 return due February 1, 2027, and adds off-cycle runs to the deposit control so each is deposited the next business day with its payday.

No Form 2848 or Form 8821 is on file for F1 Finance. Until Celeste Whitford signs a Form 2848 for Form 941, 2026 periods, F1 Finance cannot discuss the account with the IRS or file Form 843 for HANGS; the reply itself is signed and mailed by HANGS.

Unsigned draft. The reply to notice CP207 dated October 26, 2026 is due Thursday, December 10, 2026, at the address on the paper notice, by certified mail. Form 843 is filled in but held: it is filed only if a penalty is assessed after the reply. Nothing has been signed, mailed or paid.

rules.question: What does notice CP207 ask for, and by when?
rules.whyItMatters: CP207 is the IRS's request for a valid record of federal tax liability. A reply inside 45 days lets the IRS figure the penalty on the actual paydays instead of the averaged ones.
rules.effective: The IRS page on notice CP207, questions updated September 19, 2025.
rules.excerpt: We are notifying you that your deposit schedule, the record of federal tax liability (ROFTL), contains missing or incorrect information. ... Complete a new ROFTL and mail to the address at the top of your notice within 45 days of the date on your notice. ... If you're on a semi-weekly schedule, list the tax liability amount for each pay date. Report only liabilities, not your deposits.
matchPhrases: your deposit schedule, the record of federal tax liability (roftl), contains missing or incorrect information
complete a new roftl and mail to the address at the top of your notice within 45 days of the date on your notice
if you're on a semi-weekly schedule, list the tax liability amount for each pay date
report only liabilities, not your deposits
check that the total amount on your roftl schedule matches the total tax liability on your return
rules.pageOrSection: What this notice is about; What you need to do; Frequently asked questions
rules.ruleOrLimit: Mail a new record of federal tax liability within 45 days of the notice date. A semiweekly depositor lists the liability for each pay date, liabilities only, totalling the return's tax.
rules.hangsApplication: The notice is dated October 26, 2026, so the reply is due December 10, 2026. The draft Schedule B lists the liability of each of the seven Q2 paydays, $868,745.69 in all, the same as line 12; June 26 carries the regular and the off-cycle bonus run paid that day together.
rules.unresolved: The reply address is on the paper notice in the client's tax file; the transcription does not repeat it.

rules.question: What happens without a reply, and where does a reasonable-cause statement go?
rules.whyItMatters: Without a reply the averaged penalty stands. A late deposit can only be excused if a statement signed under penalty of perjury goes with the reply.
rules.effective: The IRS page on notice CP207, questions updated September 19, 2025.
rules.excerpt: We'll figure a penalty by averaging the total tax liability across the tax period. We'll apply your deposits to the average liabilities in the order we receive them. ... We can't consider requests to remove deposit penalties unless we have a correct ROFTL. If you believe you had reasonable cause for making a deposit late, include a statement signed under penalty of perjury with your reply.
matchPhrases: we'll figure a penalty by averaging the total tax liability across the tax period
we'll apply your deposits to the average liabilities in the order we receive them
we can't consider requests to remove deposit penalties unless we have a correct roftl
if you believe you had reasonable cause for making a deposit late, include a statement signed under penalty of perjury with your reply
if your response is late, we'll assess the penalty and then review your response to adjust the penalty as needed
rules.pageOrSection: What will happen if I don't reply?; I was unable to make one of the deposits on time
rules.ruleOrLimit: No reply: the averaged penalty is assessed. Relief for a late deposit is considered only with a correct ROFTL, and a reasonable-cause statement must be signed under penalty of perjury.
rules.hangsApplication: The reply carries the Schedule B first. The statement for the June 26 bonus run's late deposit is drafted for the President's signature under penalty of perjury and is sent only if a person decides to ask for reasonable cause.
rules.unresolved: Whether to send the reasonable-cause statement at all is RESIDUAL-01.

rules.question: Was HANGS a monthly or a semiweekly schedule depositor in 2026?
rules.whyItMatters: The deposit schedule decides each payday's due date and whether line 16 or Schedule B is the record of liability. The notice says semiweekly; the return said monthly.
rules.excerpt: If you're a Form 941 filer, your deposit schedule for a calendar year is determined from the total taxes reported on Forms 941, line 12, in a 4-quarter lookback period. ... If you reported $50,000 or less of taxes for the lookback period, you're a monthly schedule depositor; if you reported more than $50,000, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor. Table 1. Lookback Period for Calendar Year 2026: July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.

if you reported $50,000 or less of taxes for the lookback period, you're a monthly schedule depositor; if you reported more than $50,000, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor
lookback period for calendar year 2026
your deposit schedule isn't determined by how often you pay your employees or make deposits
rules.pageOrSection: Section 11, When To Deposit: Lookback period; Table 1
rules.ruleOrLimit: Form 941 line 12 for July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025: $50,000 or less makes a monthly depositor for 2026; more than $50,000 a semiweekly depositor.
rules.hangsApplication: Line 12 for Q3 2024 to Q2 2025 totals $2,764,880.28 ($618,734.09, $731,860.47, $672,903.17 and $741,382.55), far over $50,000: HANGS was a semiweekly depositor for all of 2026. The notice is right about the schedule; the monthly box on line 16 was wrong.

rules.unresolved: The line 12 figures are the controller's summary of the IRS account (Q1 2026, $708,472.08, is the payroll's own Q1 return); a person may confirm the lookback quarters on the IRS transcript.

rules.question: Which lookback period applies for 2026, and what must a semiweekly depositor file with Form 941?
rules.whyItMatters: A semiweekly depositor files Schedule B with every Form 941; checking the monthly box on line 16 instead is what drew the notice.
rules.excerpt: For 2026, the lookback period begins July 1, 2024, and ends June 30, 2025. ... If you reported more than $50,000 of taxes for the lookback period, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor. Check the third box on line 16. You must complete Schedule B (Form 941) and submit it with your Form 941. ... If you’re a monthly schedule depositor and accumulate a $100,000 tax liability on any day during the deposit period, you become a semiweekly schedule depositor on the next day and remain so for at least the rest of the calendar year and for the following calendar year.
matchPhrases: for 2026, the lookback period begins july 1, 2024, and ends june 30, 2025
if you reported more than $50,000 of taxes for the lookback period, you're a semiweekly schedule depositor. check the third box on line 16
you must complete schedule b (form 941) and submit it with your form 941
you become a semiweekly schedule depositor on the next day and remain so for at least the rest of the calendar year and for the following calendar year
rules.ruleOrLimit: For 2026 the lookback period is July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. A semiweekly depositor checks the third box on line 16 and attaches Schedule B. A $100,000 day also makes a monthly depositor semiweekly from the next day.
rules.hangsApplication: The Q2 return checked the monthly box and attached no Schedule B: the payroll system's May 4 upgrade had reset its Form 941 setting to monthly, and it still says monthly (Q3-01). Apart from the lookback period, every 2026 payday carried $100,000 or more of tax, which on its own makes an employer a semiweekly depositor.

rules.question: When was each Q2 deposit due?
rules.whyItMatters: Every deposit is tested against its own due date. A payday carrying $100,000 or more of tax is due the next business day, not on the semiweekly date; the IRS's averaged Wednesday shares, each under $100,000, fall on the semiweekly schedule.
rules.excerpt: Under the semiweekly deposit schedule, deposit employment taxes for payments made on Wednesday, Thursday, and/or Friday by the following Wednesday. ... If you accumulate $100,000 or more in taxes on any day during a monthly or semiweekly deposit period ..., you must deposit the tax by the next business day, whether you’re a monthly or semiweekly schedule depositor. ... A business day is any day other than a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. ... If any of the 3 weekdays after the end of a semiweekly period is a legal holiday, you’ll have an additional day for each day that is a legal holiday to make the required deposit. ... The deposit rules are based on the dates when wages are paid (cash basis) ... May 25—Memorial Day ... June 19—Juneteenth National Independence Day ... July 3—Independence Day (observed)

if any of the 3 weekdays after the end of a semiweekly period is a legal holiday, you'll have an additional day for each day that is a legal holiday to make the required deposit

rules.pageOrSection: Section 11, Depositing Taxes: semiweekly deposit schedule; $100,000 Next-Day Deposit Rule; Deposits Due on Business Days Only; legal holidays for 2026
rules.ruleOrLimit: Taxes of $100,000 or more accumulated on a day are due the next business day. Otherwise Wednesday to Friday paydays are due the following Wednesday, with one more business day for each District of Columbia legal holiday among the three weekdays after the semiweekly period. Deposits follow the dates wages are paid.
rules.hangsApplication: All seven Q2 paydays were Fridays carrying $100,000 or more of tax ($108,546.11 to $141,528.84), so each was due the next business day, the following Monday. June 26 carried the regular run ($121,321.24) and the off-cycle bonus run ($20,207.60) together, $141,528.84, all due Monday, June 29. The averaged Wednesday shares are each under $100,000 and fall on the semiweekly schedule; Memorial Day moved the May 20 share to Thursday, May 28.

rules.question: Why did the IRS propose an averaged penalty?
rules.whyItMatters: When a semiweekly depositor fills in line 16 instead of Schedule B, the IRS cannot see the paydays, so it spreads the tax evenly and tests the deposits against that.
rules.excerpt: The IRS may also assess an "averaged" FTD penalty of 2% to 10% if you're a semiweekly schedule depositor and your tax liability shown on Form 941, line 12 ... equaled or exceeded $2,500 and you: Completed Form 941, line 16, instead of Schedule B (Form 941) ... Then we apply your deposits and payments to the averaged liabilities in the date order we received your deposits.
matchPhrases: the irs may also assess an "averaged" ftd penalty of 2% to 10% if you're a semiweekly schedule depositor
completed form 941, line 16, instead of schedule b (form 941)
then we apply your deposits and payments to the averaged liabilities in the date order we received your deposits
your deposits and payments may not be counted as timely because the actual dates of your tax liabilities can't be accurately determined
rules.ruleOrLimit: A semiweekly depositor with $2,500 or more of tax who completes line 16 instead of Schedule B may be charged an averaged penalty of 2% to 10%.
rules.hangsApplication: Line 12 was $868,745.69 and the return showed only monthly totals, so the averaged penalty applied: the notice proposes $4,534.32.

rules.question: How exactly does the IRS average a semiweekly depositor's monthly liabilities?
rules.whyItMatters: Recomputing the notice's figure the IRS's way shows where it comes from, and shows that the difference from the correct penalty is the averaging itself.
rules.effective: IRM 20.1.4, Exhibit 20.1.4-3 and section 20.1.4.18, as published on irs.gov.
rules.excerpt: Monthly liability schedule provided- semi-weekly depositors: Divide each month's tax liability by 4. Assign the resulting tax liabilities to the first four Wednesdays of each month. ... Master File computes a proposed penalty by averaging the tax and generates a CP 207 or CP 207L notice (proposed averaged penalty) ... If the taxpayer provides a completed ROFTL schedule: compute the penalty based on the taxpayer's figures.
matchPhrases: monthly liability schedule provided- semi-weekly depositors: divide each month's tax liability by 4. assign the resulting tax liabilities to the first four wednesdays of each month
master file computes a proposed penalty by averaging the tax and generates a cp 207 or cp 207l notice (proposed averaged penalty)
if the taxpayer provides a completed roftl schedule: compute the penalty based on the taxpayer's figures
rules.ruleOrLimit: Monthly schedule given by a semiweekly depositor: each month's liability is split in four and placed on the month's first four Wednesdays. A completed ROFTL replaces the averaged figures.
rules.hangsApplication: Splitting April, May and June into quarters on the first four Wednesdays and applying the deposits as made gives $4,534.32, the notice's figure to the cent. On the actual paydays the penalty is $1,010.38.
rules.unresolved: The IRS's own computation is not shown on the notice; matching it to the cent is the run's evidence that this is the method used.

rules.question: What goes on the Schedule B sent with the reply?
rules.whyItMatters: The IRS refigures the penalty from the Schedule B, so each liability must sit on the day the wages were paid and the total must equal line 12.

If you have been assessed a failure-to-deposit (FTD) penalty, you may be able to file an amended Schedule B. ... The IRS will refigure the penalty and notify you of any change in the penalty.

rules.ruleOrLimit: Schedule B shows liabilities on the dates wages were paid, never deposits, and its total equals line 12.
rules.hangsApplication: Seven liabilities on seven paydays (April 3 and 17; May 1, 15 and 29; June 12 and 26), $868,745.69, equal to line 12 and to the deposits. June 26 is one entry, $141,528.84: the regular and the bonus runs paid that day.

rules.question: What does the law charge for a late deposit, and what excuses it?
rules.whyItMatters: The rate depends on how many days late each deposit was; the statute itself excuses a failure due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect.
rules.effective: 26 U.S.C. 6656 as published by Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute.
rules.excerpt: Unless it is shown that such failure is due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect, there shall be imposed upon such person a penalty equal to the applicable percentage of the amount of the underpayment. ... (i) 2 percent if the failure is for not more than 5 days, (ii) 5 percent if the failure is for more than 5 days but not more than 15 days, and (iii) 10 percent if the failure is for more than 15 days.
matchPhrases: unless it is shown that such failure is due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect
(i) 2 percent if the failure is for not more than 5 days, (ii) 5 percent if the failure is for more than 5 days but not more than 15 days, and (iii) 10 percent if the failure is for more than 15 days
a deposit made under this section shall be applied to the most recent period or periods within the specified tax period to which the deposit relates
rules.ruleOrLimit: 2% if not more than 5 days late, 5% if 6 to 15 days, 10% if more than 15 days; deposits apply to the most recent period unless designated.
rules.hangsApplication: The June 26 bonus run's $20,207.60 was deposited July 7, 8 days after its June 29 due date: 5%, $1,010.38. Applying deposits to the most recent liability keeps the late amount on the bonus run alone; the regular run's June 29 deposit was on time.

rules.question: Are days late counted in business days or calendar days?
rules.whyItMatters: Eight calendar days late is the 5% tier; counting business days would wrongly give 2%.
rules.effective: The IRS page on the failure to deposit penalty.
rules.excerpt: We calculate the amount of the Failure to Deposit Penalty based on the number of calendar days your deposit is late, starting from its due date. The penalty amounts don't add up.
matchPhrases: we calculate the amount of the failure to deposit penalty based on the number of calendar days your deposit is late, starting from its due date
the penalty amounts don't add up
rules.ruleOrLimit: Count calendar days from the due date; the tiers replace one another, they do not add.
rules.hangsApplication: June 29 to July 7 is 8 calendar days (5 business days, because July 3 was a legal holiday), so 5%, not 2% and not 7%.

rules.question: Is First Time Abate available for a Q2 2026 deposit penalty, and does HANGS's history qualify?
rules.whyItMatters: For 2026 quarterly returns the IRS no longer considers First Time Abate; it applies the Automatic Exemption from Penalty instead, on the same three-year (twelve-quarter) clean history. A prior penalty abated for reasonable cause does not spoil the history.
rules.effective: IRS page on administrative penalty relief, updated October 22, 2026.
rules.excerpt: AEP begins summer 2026. Under AEP, if you file or pay late in the current year but have timely filed returns and paid tax due for the three prior years (or 12 consecutive quarters for quarterly filers), you won't be assessed a penalty. ... 2025 tax year returns, and subsequent 2026 quarterly returns, and subsequent ... The same return type, as the original return, was timely filed for the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters), and either no penalty (except the estimated tax penalty) was assessed or a penalty was assessed, but later abated for reasonable cause or IRS error ... The IRS did not waive the failure to deposit penalty four or more times during the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters), and the failure to deposit penalty was not charged for Electronic Federal Tax Payment System (EFTPS) avoidance.
matchPhrases: aep begins summer 2026
2025 tax year returns, and subsequent 2026 quarterly returns, and subsequent
the same return type, as the original return, was timely filed for the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters)
a penalty was assessed, but later abated for reasonable cause or irs error
the irs did not waive the failure to deposit penalty four or more times during the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters)
applies to eligible 2025 tax year and 2026 quarterly returns (not considered for aep), plus all prior years/periods
if you receive a notice showing an assessed penalty but believe you should have qualified for this relief, contact us
rules.pageOrSection: Automatic exemption from penalty (AEP); How to qualify for the relief; Comparing FTA and AEP
rules.ruleOrLimit: 2026 quarterly returns get AEP, not FTA: no deposit penalty if the same return was timely filed for the prior 12 quarters with no penalty (or one abated for reasonable cause or IRS error), fewer than four FTD waivers and no EFTPS avoidance.
rules.hangsApplication: Q2 2023 to Q1 2026: all twelve Forms 941 on time, all paid, all deposits by EFTPS. The only penalty, Q1 2024's $2,372.18, was abated for reasonable cause, which the page says does not count. On the client's records the history qualifies, so the reply asks that any penalty left after the Schedule B be removed under AEP.
hangsFactsUsed: Form 941 account history, Q2 2023 to Q1 2026
rules.unresolved: AEP is applied when the original return completes processing; no AEP letter came for Q2, and the CP207's averaged penalty is only proposed. Whether the IRS will apply AEP to the remaining $1,010.38 after the Schedule B, and the count of FTD waivers in the IRS's own records, are AEP-01.

rules.question: What are the IRS's First Time Abate criteria for a deposit penalty, and which comes first, the waiver or reasonable cause?
rules.whyItMatters: The waiver looks only at the same return type, counts a prior First Time Abate against the taxpayer, and is applied before reasonable cause; it is never used when the taxpayer in fact complied.
rules.excerpt: IRS provides administrative relief from the following penalties ... Failure to Deposit (FTD) penalty under IRC 6656. ... When determining if FTA criteria are met, the criteria below applies to the same MFT as the penalized MFT ... A total of four or more FTD penalty waiver codes are present in the taxpayer's three-year penalty history. ... Penalty relief under administrative waivers, including FTA, is to be considered and applied before reasonable cause. ... Do not provide relief under the FTA waiver if there is clear and convincing evidence that the taxpayer did in fact comply.
matchPhrases: failure to deposit (ftd) penalty under irc 6656
the criteria below applies to the same mft as the penalized mft
a total of four or more ftd penalty waiver codes are present in the taxpayer's three-year penalty history
penalty relief under administrative waivers, including fta, is to be considered and applied before reasonable cause
do not provide relief under the fta waiver if there is clear and convincing evidence that the taxpayer did in fact comply
rules.ruleOrLimit: FTA (and AEP after it) tests the same return type over the prior three years; a waiver comes before reasonable cause; where the taxpayer actually complied the penalty is corrected, not waived.
rules.hangsApplication: So the order of the reply is: correct the averaged penalty with the Schedule B (HANGS complied on every regular payday), ask for administrative relief on the one late deposit, and keep reasonable cause as the fallback. The Q1 2024 abatement was for reasonable cause, not FTA, so it does not count.
hangsFactsUsed: Form 941 account history, Q2 2023 to Q1 2026
rules.unresolved: The FTD waiver codes are in the IRS's records, not the client's; a person can confirm them on the account transcript once Form 2848 is filed (POA-01).

rules.question: Would the June 26 bonus deposit qualify for reasonable cause if administrative relief is refused?
rules.whyItMatters: A run left out of the automatic deposit batch is an oversight; the IRS says mistakes and reliance on others generally do not qualify on their own.
rules.effective: IRS page on penalty relief for reasonable cause.
rules.excerpt: Reasonable cause is determined on a case-by-case basis considering all the facts and circumstances of your situation. ... For businesses, the reasons apply to the person with authority to submit the return, deposit, or tax. ... Reliance on a tax professional. You're generally responsible for complying with tax law even if someone else handles your taxes. ... Mistakes and oversights. You're responsible for making sure your tax returns, payments and deposits are correct and on time. In certain cases, reasonable cause may apply to a mistake if additional facts and circumstances show that you tried to comply with tax law.
matchPhrases: reasonable cause is determined on a case-by-case basis considering all the facts and circumstances of your situation
for businesses, the reasons apply to the person with authority to submit the return, deposit, or tax
you're generally responsible for complying with tax law even if someone else handles your taxes

rules.pageOrSection: Failure to file or pay penalties; factors that don't generally qualify
rules.ruleOrLimit: Case by case. Reliance on others and mistakes generally do not qualify, unless other facts show the business tried to comply.
rules.hangsApplication: The facts for HANGS: twelve clean quarters, every regular deposit on time, the missed run caught by the controller's own July reconciliation and deposited in full 8 days late. That is a fair statement but not a strong reasonable-cause case; it is the fallback only.
rules.unresolved: Whether to send the reasonable-cause statement, and the President's signature under penalty of perjury, are RESIDUAL-01.
